findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/ceil to a datetime, so every non-empty page raises
findings.body: The audit log endpoint sends `order_by="-datetime"`, so `self.key` is `datetime` and `getattr(item, self.key)` returns a datetime. `math.floor(datetime)` and `math.ceil(datetime)` raise TypeError. `build_cursor` and `_build_next_values` call `key(results[0])` whenever results exist, so any request with `?optimized_pagination=true` from an admin with a non-empty audit log returns a 500. `DateTimePaginator.get_item_key` converts datetimes to a timestamp first; this class does not. `value_from_cursor` also returns the raw int cursor value, which `build_queryset` would compare against a datetime column. The path is untested (no test covers `OptimizedCursorPaginator` or the endpoint flag), which is why this was not caught.

findings.title: Negative cursor offsets are passed straight to queryset slicing, which Django rejects
findings.body: When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django QuerySets raise AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported') for negative slice bounds, so any caller who supplies a cursor string such as `0:-1:0` gets a 500. The `Cursor` parser accepts negative offsets from the client, so this is reachable by any user for whom the flag is on (superusers or members with global access). The comments on this branch say it 'enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds' and that 'permissions are checked at the queryset level'. Neither is true: the queryset is only filtered by organization_id, and negative slicing cannot be executed.

findings.title: Unrelated, undocumented pagination switch added to the audit log endpoint
findings.body: This PR is about the spans buffer, but it adds an `optimized_pagination` query parameter to the audit log endpoint that routes to the new paginator. Enabling it for superusers and has_global_access members turns on the negative-offset path (see paginator.py line 877), which crashes. The parameter is not validated by the serializer, has no tests, and is not documented. The duplicated `paginate` call also means the endpoint has two code paths to keep in sync. This change should be split out and either removed or fixed and tested separately.

findings.title: Switching span-buf:s:* from Redis sets to sorted sets breaks in-flight keys during deploy
findings.body: The key names `span-buf:s:{...}` are unchanged, but the type changes from SET (`sadd`/`sscan`) to ZSET (`zadd`/`zscan`). Keys written by the old code remain in Redis for up to `redis_ttl` (3600s) and are still being read and written. During that window, `p.zadd` here raises WRONGTYPE for any group whose key already holds a set. The pipeline `execute()` raises on the first error by default, so the whole batch fails and the consumer retries or crashes. The flusher's `p.zscan` at line 434 fails the same way on old set keys. There is no key versioning or migration step to prevent this.

findings.title: ZUNIONSTORE uses default SUM aggregation, so re-delivered spans get doubled scores
findings.body: `zunionstore` defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`. When the same span payload exists in both the source and destination sets (for example, Kafka redelivers a span), its score becomes 2x the end timestamp. The score is the eviction key for `zpopmin`, so duplicated spans are treated as the newest and are never evicted, and eviction order is wrong for those members. The same problem applies to the second `zunionstore` at line 53. Using `AGGREGATE MIN` or `MAX` would keep the timestamp. This only matters once a segment exceeds 1000 spans, but the eviction is the feature this PR adds.

findings.title: Span eviction silently truncates segments and removes the old max_segment_spans guard
findings.body: Previously, `_load_segment_data` skipped segments over `max_segment_spans` and logged an error plus a metric. That check is removed in this PR, and the Lua script now `zpopmin`s the oldest spans beyond 1000 with no log or metric. Flushed segments are now silently incomplete. The Python limit `max_segment_spans` (default 1001 in buffer.py line 150) is now dead, and it disagrees with the hard-coded 1000 in the script. Operators have no way to see or tune the eviction. At minimum, the eviction should emit a counter, and the cap should come from configuration.

findings.title: Redirect-chain depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 and its explanatory comment removed
findings.body: The loop bound changes from 10000 to 1000, and the comment that documented the depth limit and its consequence is deleted. Redirect chains deeper than 1000 will now stop resolving early, so their spans land in a separate segment instead of being joined. This is unrelated to the eviction work and is not mentioned anywhere in the PR.

findings.title: Comment claims negative offsets are now allowed, but no code changed
findings.body: The added comment says the Cursor 'Allow[s] negative offsets for advanced pagination' and 'enables efficient reverse pagination'. The only change in this hunk is the comment, and `self.offset = int(offset)` is unchanged. Downstream, Django slicing rejects negative bounds, so the comment describes a capability that does not exist.

findings.title: Comment says negative offsets are safe and efficient, but they are clamped or crash
findings.body: The comment says negative offsets are allowed for 'efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning' and that 'this is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions'. The code clamps negative offsets to 0 for next-page cursors, which silently changes the result. For previous-page cursors (`is_prev`), `offset` is still passed unclamped, so a negative value raises AssertionError from Django. The comment misstates both the behavior and the safety.

findings.title: No test exercises the eviction that this PR is about
findings.body: The PR is titled 'eviction during insert' and adds a hard 1000-span cap in the Lua script, but no test inserts more than 1000 spans into a segment. Nothing verifies that the oldest spans are evicted, that the newest are kept, that the cap holds across multiple batches, or that duplicate payloads are scored correctly (see the SUM aggregation finding). The tests only add `end_timestamp_precise` fields, so the behavior change is untested.

findings.title: Module docstring still describes span-buf:s:* as plain sets
findings.body: The glossary says `span-buf:s:*` are 'the actual set keys', and the flow description says spans are added to 'the set'. After this change they are sorted sets scored by end timestamp, and eviction depends on that ordering. Future readers will be misled about the data type, which is exactly the mismatch that breaks in-flight keys during deploy.
